The Use Case

Clinical depth and claims breadth live apart — so value-based care underperforms

Epic tells us what happened inside our walls. Claims tell us what happened everywhere else — and what it cost. Neither alone answers the questions that drive quality and performance. The strategy: unify them once, then solve specific clinical use cases on that foundation.

Clinical (Epic)

Deep, real-time detail — labs, vitals, diagnoses, meds, encounters — but only for care delivered in our network. Blind to what happens elsewhere.

Claims (Payer)

The longitudinal, cross-setting view — utilization, cost, leakage, out-of-network care — but lagged, coded, and missing clinical nuance.

The gap

Without a unified member view we can't see total cost of care, true leakage, or where quality gaps actually close. Programs run on partial truth.

What unifying unlocks

A single member spine joining clinical + claims lets us target the right patients, close gaps that matter, recapture risk accurately, keep care in-network, and prove value to payers — all from one governed source instead of disconnected spreadsheets and extracts.

The bet

Foundation first, but never foundation-only. Each increment ships a working clinical or operational capability, not just plumbing.

Strategic Approach

Solve it in thin slices, not big phases

We don't build the whole platform and then look for value. We cut a narrow vertical slice — one claims feed, Epic clinical, a unified identity — prove it end to end, then widen the data and the use-case portfolio. Each 90-day increment leaves a working capability behind.

The Data Foundation

How clinical + claims actually become one

Unification isn't a join — it's an engineered spine. The foundation resolves identity, conforms two very different data shapes, and certifies the result so every use case starts from the same truth.

Step 01

Member identity

Probabilistic + deterministic matching builds a master member/patient ID linking Epic records to claims members across payers.

Step 02

Conform shapes

Map Epic encounters and claims lines to a common model — member, encounter, diagnosis, procedure, cost — in Silver.

Step 03

Enforce quality

DLT expectations validate completeness and reconcile overlaps (e.g., a visit present in both clinical and claims).

Step 04

Certify Gold

Publish curated marts, features, and certified KPI definitions consumed by BI, ML, and agents alike.

Why this order matters

Identity first means every downstream metric — leakage, total cost of care, gap closure — is computed on a complete member journey, not a fragment. Get the spine right once and every use case inherits it.

Governed throughout

PHI controls, masking, and lineage are applied at the foundation in Unity Catalog, so use cases built on top are compliant by inheritance — not by re-implementing security per project.

Use Cases on the Foundation

From foundation to clinical quality & performance

Once the spine exists, each use case is a thin build — not a new platform. These map directly to the KPIs we're solving for.

Readmission reduction

Risk model on unified history flags high-risk discharges; care teams intervene and the score writes back to Epic. → readmissions ↓

Care-gap closure

Claims + clinical evidence identify open HEDIS gaps the EHR alone would miss, routed to outreach. → gap closure ↑

Risk recapture

Reconcile coded conditions across claims and clinical notes to recapture HCCs accurately and compliantly. → recapture ↑

Leakage management

Claims reveal out-of-network care; dashboards target referral patterns to keep care in-network. → leakage ↓

Total cost of care

Member-level cost across all settings exposes high-cost cohorts and savings opportunities. → PMPM ↓

VBC performance

One certified view of quality + cost proves performance to payers and runs the value-based care program. → all KPIs

How We Deliver

Operating model & ways of working

Incremental delivery needs an operating model to match: small cross-functional pods, product ownership of data, and engineering discipline so quality scales with scope.

Delivery pods

Each pod pairs data engineering, clinical informatics, and analytics around one use case — owning it end to end.

Data products

The foundation and certified marts are managed as products with owners, SLAs, and roadmaps — not one-off projects.

DataOps / MLOps

Git-based CI/CD, automated testing, and DLT quality gates make every pipeline and model promotable and observable.

Governance council

A cross-functional council owns PHI policy, metric definitions, and access — keeping "one source of truth" true.

Clinical partnership

Clinicians co-design every use case and validate model outputs before write-back. Adoption is engineered in from day one — insight that doesn't reach the workflow doesn't move a KPI.

Enablement & FinOps

Analyst enablement on the semantic layer drives self-service; cost monitoring and right-sizing keep elastic compute economical as workloads grow.

Risks & Guardrails

What could derail this — and how we hold the line

Identity match quality

Weak member matching corrupts every downstream metric. Guardrail: measured match rates, stewardship workflow, and human review thresholds before Gold publishes.

PHI & compliance

Claims + clinical together raise sensitivity. Guardrail: Unity Catalog masking, minimum-necessary access, BAA-backed services, and full audit from day one.

Claims data lag

Claims arrive 30–90 days late, limiting real-time use. Guardrail: design use cases for the data's cadence; pair lagging claims with real-time clinical signals.

Adoption & trust

Unused insight moves nothing. Guardrail: clinician co-design, write-back into existing workflow, and certified single-definition metrics to retire "two numbers."

Summary · The Ask

One foundation, four increments, six KPIs

The strategy

Unify Epic clinical + payer claims on an Azure Databricks lakehouse, then solve prioritized clinical quality and operational performance use cases on that foundation.

The approach

Four 90-day increments, each shipping a working capability and moving a KPI — foundation first, but never foundation-only.

The decision

Option C — Databricks Lakehouse — chosen over extending legacy or a native-only warehouse, on unification, AI, governance, and TCO.
